summary: FCFS SAVI is a mechanism for source address validation in IPv6 networks. The first node to use a locally assigned address is the one allowed to keep using it, and others are blocked. It complements ingress filtering to help detect and prevent source address spoofing.

plainLanguage.summary: FCFS SAVI lets a switch check that a host on the local link is really using its own IPv6 address. The switch records the port where an address was first used and drops later packets that use that address from a different port. The hosts themselves need no changes.

subtitle: A way for switches to check that hosts on a local IPv6 link are really using their own source addresses.

tldr.problem: A host on an IPv6 link can send packets with a source address that belongs to somebody else, and ingress filtering only checks traffic that arrives from another network.
tldr.mechanism: A switch or router running FCFS SAVI binds each source address to the switch port where it was first used, confirms the claim with Neighbor Discovery messages, and drops later packets that carry that address from a different port.
tldr.outcome: No change is needed on the hosts and it complements ingress filtering, but the method is only as strong as its binding anchor, which must be a switch port, and it relies on hosts defending their own addresses.

today: RFC 6620 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC leaves DHCP-assigned addresses to a separate mechanism, and recommends the SEND-based mechanism where Secure Neighbor Discovery is deployed.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6620 defines FCFS SAVI, the First-Come, First-Served Source Address Validation Improvement. It is a mechanism that provides source address validation for IPv6 networks using the FCFS principle. The RFC states that the mechanism is intended to complement ingress filtering techniques to help detect and prevent source address spoofing.

The design rests on one rule. The first host to use a locally assigned address is the owner of that address until further notice, and packets that later carry the same source address are dropped unless they come from the same place. No change is required on the hosts, because the checking uses protocols that hosts already run.
sections.plainLanguage: FCFS SAVI lets a switch check that a host on the link is really using its own IPv6 address. The switch records the port where each address was first used and drops later packets that use it from a different port. The hosts themselves need no changes.

sections.title: Scope: Traffic That Starts on the Link
sections.content:
The application scenario for FCFS SAVI is limited to the local link. Hosts generate packets with their own address as the source address, and the RFC calls this local traffic. Routers forward packets that other hosts generated, so the source address in a forwarded packet is not the router's own. The RFC calls this transit traffic.

FCFS SAVI validates local traffic only. Verifying transit traffic is out of scope, and the RFC recommends ingress filtering (RFC 2827) for that job. Because FCFS SAVI relies on ingress filtering to validate transit traffic while adding validation for local traffic, the two techniques together raise the security level.

The RFC is designed for locally assigned IPv6 addresses, in particular addresses configured through Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 4862). Manually configured addresses can be supported as well, with manual configuration of the binding on the FCFS SAVI device giving higher security. Addresses assigned by DHCPv6 can also be used, since they ought to run the Duplicate Address Detection procedure, although a mechanism tailored to DHCP-assigned addresses is defined in a separate document.
sections.plainLanguage: FCFS SAVI only checks traffic that starts on the local link. Traffic forwarded by a router is checked by other means, such as ingress filtering. It is meant for IPv6 addresses that hosts set up themselves, mainly through stateless autoconfiguration.

sections.title: Address Ownership and Binding Anchors
sections.content:
The main function of FCFS SAVI is to verify that the source address used in data packets actually belongs to the originator of the packet. To define that, the RFC defines address ownership: a host owns an address if it is entitled to send packets with that address as the source.

Ownership is decided on the First-Come, First-Served principle. The first host that claims a given source address is the owner of the address until further notice. The device running the FCFS SAVI function records the claim by binding the source address to a binding anchor, which consists of Layer 2 information that the device already has, such as the port in a switched LAN. Subsequent data packets containing that source address are checked against the same binding anchor.

A host that moves from one segment of a LAN to another segment of the same subnetwork keeps its IP address but may reach the network through a different binding anchor. FCFS SAVI copes with this by using the Neighbor Discovery protocol (RFC 4861) to test whether the host is still reachable using the previous anchor. If it is not, FCFS SAVI assumes the new location is valid and creates a new binding. If the host is still reachable through the previous anchor, packets arriving from the new anchor are dropped.

The RFC is explicit that only switch ports may be used as binding anchors. A solution is not stronger than its binding anchor, so an anchor that is easily spoofable, such as a MAC address, makes the solution weak. Other forms of binding anchor are out of scope and need their own analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is that the first host to use an address keeps the right to use it. The switch remembers which port that host is on and checks later packets against that port. If the host moves to another port, the switch asks whether it is still reachable at the old port and updates the record if it is not.

sections.title: The Protection Perimeter and the Two Port Types
sections.content:
FCFS SAVI provides perimetrical security. The FCFS SAVI devices form what the RFC calls an FCFS SAVI protection perimeter, and they verify that any packet crossing the perimeter is compliant. Once a packet is inside the perimeter, no further validation is performed on it.

Each FCFS SAVI device therefore has two types of port. Validating Ports run FCFS SAVI processing and filtering on the packets they receive. Hosts are normally connected to them, as are non-SAVI switches that sit outside the perimeter. Trusted Ports run no FCFS SAVI processing at all, and packets received on them are not validated. They are used for connections with trusted infrastructure: other FCFS SAVI devices, routers, and switches that carry only trusted nodes.

Storing a binding for every source address in the subnetwork on every device would impose a significant memory burden, so the binding state is distributed. Each device stores only the bindings whose anchors correspond to interfaces that connect to the part of the topology outside the perimeter, so the binding for a source address is stored in the first FCFS SAVI device that the packet reaches. The distributed state must stay coherent, or the same source address could end up bound to different anchors on different devices, which would allow two hosts to send packets with the same source address.

To keep the state coherent, the devices use the Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages of Neighbor Discovery. Before creating a local binding, a device sends a Neighbor Solicitation for the address involved. If a host replies with a Neighbor Advertisement, the device infers that a binding for that address exists on another FCFS SAVI device and creates no local binding. If no reply arrives, the device infers that no binding exists elsewhere and creates the local binding.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the ports facing untrusted parts of the network are checked. The switch keeps records for the addresses it has seen on those ports only, which limits memory use. To keep the records consistent across several switches, a switch asks on the network whether an address is already in use before it records one.

sections.title: Processing Transit Traffic and Local Traffic
sections.content:
The FCFS SAVI function is located in a forwarding device, such as a router or a Layer 2 switch. A data packet received through a Trusted Port is forwarded and no SAVI processing is performed on it. A packet received through a Validating Port is classified first: the device checks whether the source address of the packet belongs to one of the directly connected prefixes available on the receiving interface, by searching the FCFS SAVI Prefix List.

If the source address does not belong to an on-link prefix of the receiving port, the packet is transit traffic and SHOULD be discarded. If discarding is not acceptable, logging or triggering alarms MAY be used instead. The device MAY also send an ICMP Destination Unreachable error back to the source address, using ICMPv6 code 5, which means the source address failed an ingress or egress policy. If the source address does belong to a prefix available on the receiving port, the local traffic validation process runs. A packet whose source address is an unspecified address is forwarded with no SAVI processing, except for the Neighbor Solicitation messages involved in Duplicate Address Detection.

The FCFS SAVI Prefix List contains the set of on-link IPv6 prefixes and the interface where each prefix is directly connected. An FCFS SAVI device MUST support manual configuration of this list, which is useful when no prefixes are advertised on the link. It MUST also support discovery of on-link prefixes from Router Advertisement messages received on Trusted Ports, following the procedure a host uses for Prefix Information options in RFC 4861, with the prefixes going into the FCFS SAVI Prefix List instead of the ND Prefix List. When the device boots it MUST send a Router Solicitation with the unspecified source address.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet from a checked port is first sorted into two kinds. A packet whose source address is not from this link was forwarded by a router, so it is dropped or reported. A packet whose source address belongs to this link is checked against the switch's binding records.

sections.title: The Binding State Machine
sections.content:
Local traffic, both control and data packets, is processed with a state machine that applies to one source address at a time. The state holds the IP address, the binding anchor P, and a lifetime LT. The possible states are NO_BIND, TENTATIVE, VALID, TESTING_TP-LT and TESTING_VP. After bootstrapping, when no binding exists, every address is in NO_BIND.

In NO_BIND, a Duplicate Address Detection Neighbor Solicitation (DAD_NS) or a data packet arriving on a Validating Port moves the state to TENTATIVE, sets the anchor to that port and sets the lifetime to TENT_LT. When a data packet arrives, the device SHOULD run the Duplicate Address Detection procedure on the host's behalf, sending 2 Neighbor Solicitation messages with DupAddrDetectTransmits set to 2 and RetransTimer set to T_WAIT milliseconds. It MUST NOT forward the data packets until the binding has been verified, though it MAY store them instead of discarding them.

In TENTATIVE, if the lifetime times out the state becomes VALID, the lifetime is set to DEFAULT_LT, and any stored data packets are forwarded. A Neighbor Advertisement received through a Trusted Port with that target address returns the state to NO_BIND, clears the binding anchor and the lifetime, and discards the stored data packets.

In VALID, a data packet from the bound Validating Port is forwarded and the lifetime is set to DEFAULT_LT again. A DAD_NS through a Trusted Port, or an expiring lifetime, moves the state to TESTING_TP-LT. A data packet, a DAD_NS or a DAD_NA arriving on a different Validating Port moves the state to TESTING_VP, and the device then tests which anchor is the genuine one. In TESTING_TP-LT, a Neighbor Advertisement on the bound port or a data packet on that port makes the binding VALID again, while an expiring lifetime clears the binding. In TESTING_VP, the anchor moves to the port where the traffic was seen, and the binding becomes VALID when the lifetime expires or a Neighbor Advertisement arrives on the original port.

The FCFS SAVI device MUST join the solicited node multicast group for all the addresses in a state other than NO_BIND. Relying on the host behind the Validating Port to do so is not enough, because the node may move and the multicast traffic for that group would then no longer reach the device.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address goes through a small number of states. It starts unknown, becomes tentative while the switch checks the claim, and then valid. If traffic for the same address turns up on a different port, the switch tests the two places and keeps the one that answers.

sections.title: Default Values and Port Configuration
sections.content:
The specification defines three default values. TENT_LT is 500 milliseconds, DEFAULT_LT is 5 minutes, and T_WAIT is 250 milliseconds. An implementation MAY allow these values to be modified, but tuning them precisely is considered out of the scope of the document.

Port configuration follows from the perimeter model. The FCFS SAVI realm, the part of the topology inside the protection perimeter, MUST be connected, or legitimate transit traffic may be dropped. Ports connected to another FCFS SAVI device MUST be configured as Trusted Ports, because doing otherwise significantly increases the memory consumed by the FCFS SAVI devices and may result in legitimate transit traffic being dropped. Ports connected to routers MUST also be Trusted Ports. Ports connected to hosts SHOULD be Validating Ports, and untrusted hosts MUST be connected to Validating Ports; a trusted host such as a server may sit on a Trusted Port. A chain of one or more legacy switches that has hosts attached SHOULD be behind a Validating Port, while a chain that carries other FCFS SAVI devices and routers but no hosts MUST be behind a Trusted Port.

If the FCFS SAVI device is a switch that supports customer VLANs, the FCFS SAVI implementation MUST behave as if there were one FCFS SAVI process per customer VLAN. Each process stores the binding information for the nodes attached to that particular VLAN.
sections.plainLanguage: Three timers control how long the switch waits before it accepts an address as genuine or gives up on it. The document also says which ports to check and which to leave alone, and it says a switch with VLANs runs a separate check for each VLAN.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Two kinds of denial-of-service attack are considered. An attacker can send packets with many different source addresses to make the device create state for each of them and waste memory. The RFC recommends that when the memory allocated for the FCFS SAVI database runs out, new entries are created by deleting the entries with the later creation time, so older entries are preserved and newer entries overwrite each other. Entries are also collected using the lifetime, which raises the cost of the attack because the attacker has to keep sending for every address. A device should also reserve a minimum amount of memory for each port, enough for four bindings, so an attack on one port does not starve the others. The device MUST limit the memory used to store data packets, so that other functions keep memory available. Because the device generates two DAD_NS messages for each DAD_NS or data packet it receives, it can be used as an amplifier, so it MUST rate limit the messages it generates, on a per-port basis.

The RFC then lists the threats it does not remove. If an attacker manages to send packets using the binding anchor associated with an address, validation succeeds and the packet is allowed through. That can happen by forging the anchor, or by sharing it: hosts behind a legacy switch share one switch port, so they can spoof each other's addresses and the FCFS SAVI device will not detect it. The RFC assumes a host can defend its address while the Duplicate Address Detection procedure runs; an attacker who prevents the host from answering can destroy the existing binding and create a new one. A router is trusted, so a compromised router can send traffic with spoofed source addresses and it will be allowed.

For privacy, personally identifying information MUST NOT be included in the FCFS SAVI database, the MAC address being the canonical example. Compliant implementations MUST NOT log binding anchor information unless there is an identified reason why that information is likely to be involved in the detection, prevention, or tracing of actual source address spoofing. Information that is not logged MUST be deleted as soon as the state for the address is back to NO_BIND, and information about the majority of hosts that never spoof SHOULD NOT be logged.

Finally, the RFC notes that when Secure Neighbor Discovery is deployed, the FCFS SAVI device has to generate Neighbor Solicitations it cannot sign, because it does not hold the private key associated with the address. In that case the RFC recommends the SEND-based source address validation mechanism instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The attack surface is the switch's own memory and the messages it sends, so the document limits both. It also says what the method cannot do. It cannot tell two hosts behind the same legacy switch apart, and it cannot stop an attacker who stops a host from answering for its own address.
